verses.zh: 末底改知道所做的这一切事，就撕裂衣服，穿麻衣，蒙灰尘，在城中行走，痛哭哀号。
verses.en: Now when Mordecai became aware of all that had been done, he[NOTE:1] tore his garments and put on sackcloth and ashes. He went out into the city, crying out in a loud[NOTE:2] and bitter voice.
notes: Heb “Mordecai.” The pronoun (“he”) was used in the translation for stylistic reasons. A repetition of the proper name here is redundant in terms of contemporary English style.
Heb “great.”
verses.commentary:
4:1 "he tore his clothes, put on sackcloth and ashes, and went out into the midst of the city and wailed
loudly and bitterly" These were Jewish mourning rites; more are listed in Esth. 4:3:

- tore his clothes, Esth. 4:1

- put on sackcloth, Esth. 4:1,3

- put on ashes (or dust, but on the head), Esth. 4:1,3

- wailed loudly and bitterly, Esth. 4:1,3

- fasted, Esth. 4:3

- wept, Esth. 4:3

Numbers 1 and 2 are often done together (cf. Isa. 58:5; Jer. 6:26; Jonah 3:6). The Persians
also practiced #1 (cf. Herodotus, Hist. 8.99).

Special Topic: Grieving Rites

verses.zh: 到了朝门前停住脚步，因为穿麻衣的不可进朝门。
verses.en: But he went no farther than the king’s gate, for no one was permitted to enter the king’s gate clothed in sackcloth.
verses.commentary: 4:2 Expressing personal emotions in the king's presence or palace was inappropriate (cf. Neh. 2:1-2).

verses.zh: 王的谕旨所到的各省各处，犹大人大大悲哀，禁食哭泣哀号，穿麻衣躺在灰中的甚多。
verses.en: Throughout each and every province where the king’s edict and law were announced[NOTE:1] there was considerable[NOTE:2] mourning among the Jews, along with fasting, weeping, and sorrow.[NOTE:3] Sackcloth and ashes were characteristic[NOTE:4] of many.
notes: Heb “reached” (so NAB, NLT); KJV, NASB, NIV “came”; TEV “wherever the king’s proclamation was made known.”
Heb “great” (so KJV, NIV, NRSV, NLT); NAB “the Jews went into deep mourning.”

Although prayer is not specifically mentioned here, it is highly unlikely that appeals to God for help were not a part of this reaction to devastating news. As elsewhere in the book of Esther, the writer seems deliberately to keep religious actions in the background.
Heb “were spread to many”; KJV, NIV “many (+ people NLT) lay in sackcloth and ashes.”
verses.commentary:
4:3

NASB, NKJV, NJB, NIV, Peshitta
"many"

NRSV, TEV, REB
"most"

JPSOA
"everybody"

NAB
"all"

The Hebrew has "many," but this term often has the connotation of "all" (cf. Isa. 53:11,12
vs. Isa. 53:6; Rom. 5:19 vs. Rom. 5:18).

▣ "lay on sackcloth" Sackcloth was made of coarse goat or camel hair. It was rough and most
uncomfortable when worn close to the skin. The Jews wore it as an outer garment and even slept on it
(cf. 2 Sam. 21:10; 1 Kgs. 21:27; Isa. 58:5).

verses.zh: 王后以斯帖的宫女和太监来把这事告诉以斯帖，她甚是忧愁，就送衣服给末底改穿，要他脱下麻衣，他却不受。
verses.en: When Esther’s female attendants and her eunuchs came and informed her about Mordecai’s behavior,[NOTE:1] the queen was overcome with anguish. Although she sent garments for Mordecai to put on so that he could remove his sackcloth, he would not accept them.
notes: The words “about Mordecai’s behavior” are not in the Hebrew text, but are supplied in translation for the sake of clarity. Cf. NIV, NLT “about Mordecai”; TEV, CEV “what Mordecai was doing.”
verses.commentary:
4:4

NASB
"the queen writhed in great anguish"

NKJV, NRSV
"the queen was deeply distressed"

TEV
"she was deeply disturbed"

NJB
"she was overcome with grief"

JPSOA
"the queen was greatly agitated"

Peshitta
"the Queen was exceedingly disturbed"

The VERB (BDB 296 I; KB 297; Hithpalpel IMPERFECT) means
to writhe in anxiety. The term is often used of child birth (cf. Ps. 29:8; 55:4-5; Isa. 26:17; 51:2), as well
as the pain of the wicked in judgment (cf. Job 15:20).

The ADVERB "deeply" (BDB 547) is added for emphasis. This term is used for
both physical and psychological pain.

Her servants evidently knew her close relationship to Mordecai even though they may not have
known that they were blood relations. Esther was greatly concerned about her uncle's actions.

verses.zh: 以斯帖就把王所派伺候她的一个太监，名叫哈他革召来，吩咐他去见末底改，要知道这是甚么事，是甚么缘故。
verses.en: So Esther called for Hathach, one of the king’s eunuchs who had been placed at her service,[NOTE:1] and instructed him to find out the cause and reason for Mordecai’s behavior.[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “whom he caused to stand before her”; NASB “whom the king had appointed to attend her.”
Heb “concerning Mordecai, to know what this was, and why this was.”

verses.zh: 于是哈他革出到朝门前的宽阔处见末底改。
verses.en: So Hathach went to Mordecai at the plaza of the city in front of the king’s gate.

verses.zh: 末底改将自己所遇的事，并哈曼为灭绝犹大人应许捐入王库的银数都告诉了他；
verses.en: Then Mordecai related to him everything that had happened to him, even the specific amount of money that Haman had offered to pay to the king’s treasuries for the Jews to be destroyed.
verses.commentary:
4:7-8 Mordecai tells Esther's servant (Hathach) the situation and even gives him a copy of the
posted edict to show Esther.

verses.zh: 又将所抄写传遍书珊城要灭绝犹大人的旨意交给哈他革，要给以斯帖看，又要给她说明，并嘱咐她进去见王，为本族的人在王面前恳切祈求。
verses.en: He also gave him a written copy of the law that had been disseminated[NOTE:1] in Susa for their destruction so that he could show it to Esther and talk to her about it. He also gave instructions that she should go to the king to implore him and petition him on behalf of her people.
notes: Heb “given” (so KJV); NASB, NRSV, TEV, NLT “issued”; NIV “published”; NAB “promulgated.”

verses.zh: 哈他革回来，将末底改的话告诉以斯帖；
verses.en: So Hathach returned and related Mordecai’s instructions[NOTE:1] to Esther.
notes: Heb “the words of Mordecai” (so KJV); NIV, NRSV, CEV “what Mordecai had said”; NLT “with Mordecai’s message.”
verses.commentary:
4:9-12 She seemed to fear for her own life in breaking Persian court customs more than for the slaughter
of her people! We learn of some of these customs from Herodotus (Hist. 3.118,140), that only members
of the seven special Persian families could approach the king without his permission.

verses.zh: 以斯帖就吩咐哈他革去见末底改，说：
verses.en: Then Esther replied to Hathach with instructions for Mordecai:

verses.zh: 「王的一切臣仆和各省的人民都知道有一个定例：若不蒙召，擅入内院见王的，无论男女必被治死；除非王向他伸出金杖，不得存活。现在我没有蒙召进去见王已经三十日了。」
verses.en: “All the servants of the king and the people of the king’s provinces know that there is only one law applicable[NOTE:1] to any man or woman who comes uninvited to the king in the inner court—that person will be put to death, unless the king extends to him the gold scepter, permitting him to be spared.[NOTE:2] Now I have not been invited to come to the king for some 30 days.”
notes: Heb “one is his law”; NASB “he (the king NIV) has but one law”
Heb “and he will live”; KJV, ASV “that he may live”; NIV11 “and spares their lives.”

verses.zh: 人就把以斯帖这话告诉末底改。
verses.en: When Esther’s reply[NOTE:1] was conveyed to Mordecai,
notes: Heb “the words of Esther”; TEV, NLT “Esther’s message.”

verses.zh: 末底改托人回覆以斯帖说：「你莫想在王宫里强过一切犹大人，得免这祸。
verses.en: he[NOTE:1] said to take back this answer to Esther: “Don’t imagine that because you are part of the king’s household you will be the one Jew[NOTE:2] who will escape.
notes: Heb “Mordecai.” The pronoun (“he”) was used in the translation for stylistic reasons. A repetition of the proper name here is redundant in terms of contemporary English style.
Heb “from all the Jews”; KJV “more than all the Jews”; NIV “you alone of all the Jews.”
verses.commentary:
4:13 Mordecai seems to be somewhat upset at Esther's response. Mordecai plainly tells Esther that if
all the Jews die, then she will also die!

verses.zh: 此时你若闭口不言，犹大人必从别处得解脱，蒙拯救；你和你父家必致灭亡。焉知你得了王后的位分不是为现今的机会吗？」
verses.en: If you keep quiet at this time, liberation and protection for the Jews will appear[NOTE:1] from another source,[NOTE:2] while you and your father’s household perish. It may very well be[NOTE:3] that you have achieved royal status[NOTE:4] for such a time as this!”
notes: Heb “stand”; KJV, NASB, NIV, NLT “arise.”

Heb “place” (so KJV, NIV, NLT); NRSV “from another quarter.” This is probably an oblique reference to help coming from God. D. J. A. Clines disagrees; in his view a contrast between deliverance by Esther and deliverance by God is inappropriate (Ezra, Nehemiah, Esther [NCBC], 302). But Clines’ suggestion that perhaps the reference is to deliverance by Jewish officials or by armed Jewish revolt is less attractive than seeing this veiled reference as part of the literary strategy of the book, which deliberately keeps God’s providential dealings entirely in the background.
Heb “And who knows whether” (so NASB). The question is one of hope, but free of presumption. Cf. Jonah 3:9.
Heb “have come to the kingdom”; NRSV “to royal dignity”; NIV11 “to your royal position”; NLT “have been elevated to the palace.”
verses.commentary:
4:14 "relief and deliverance will arise for the Jews from another place" This is where most commentators
assert that a strong allusion to God is assumed (as in Est. 4:16, cf. the Targums and Josephus' Antiq. 11.6.7).
This is the Hebrew doctrine of God's providence. The Jews were an integral part of God's redemptive plan for
all humanity (cf. Rom. 9:4-5).

The term "relief" (BDB 926, KB 1194) has a wide semantic field (possibly reflects
two separate roots). Its primary meaning was "to be wide or spacious," but the same three consonants
can also mean

- liberation

- air, breath, wind, spirit

- smell, odor, scent

As God delivered His people from Egypt (cf. Gen. 45:5-7) He will deliver them from Haman.
Esther has been placed in a special place for God to use (like Joseph) at this critical time (i.e., the
unseen hand of God).

Special
Topic: Satanic Attempts to Thwart the Messianic Line in Genesis

▣ "you and your father's house will perish" Although Mordecai has confidence that God will deliver
His people, Esther must choose if she will allow God to work through her life. This is the biblical tension
between God's unconditional covenant (i.e., human redemption) and the conditional individual response.

Special Topic: Covenant

▣ "And who knows whether you have not attained royalty for such a time as this" This is the most
famous phrase in the book of Esther. It encourages great faith in God's unseen, but present, care and
providence (the unseen, but ever-present, hand of God)!

verses.zh: 以斯帖就吩咐人回报末底改说：
verses.en: Then Esther sent this reply to Mordecai:

verses.zh: 「你当去招聚书珊城所有的犹大人，为我禁食三昼三夜，不吃不喝；我和我的宫女也要这样禁食。然后我违例进去见王，我若死就死吧！」
verses.en: “Go, assemble all the Jews who are found in Susa, and fast on my behalf. Don’t eat and don’t drink for three days, night or day. My female attendants and I[NOTE:1] will also fast in the same way. Afterward I will go to the king, even though it violates the law.[NOTE:2] If I perish, I perish.”
notes: Heb “I and my female attendants.” The translation reverses the order for stylistic reasons.
Heb “which is not according to the law” (so KJV, NASB); NAB “contrary to the law.”
verses.commentary:
4:16 "do not eat or drink for three days" There is a series of IMPERATIVES (3) and
two IMPERFECTS used in a JUSSIVE sense.

- go (BDB 229, KB 246, Qal IMPERATIVE)

- assemble (BEB 488, KB 484, Qal IMPERATIVE)

- fast (BDB 847, KB 1012, Qal IMPERATIVE)

- do not eat (BDB 27, KB 40, Qal IMPERFECT used in a JUSSIVE sense)

- do not drink (BDB 1059, KB 1667, Qal IMPERFECT used in a
JUSSIVE sense)

This verse vividly communicates Esther's fear ad faith!

Although prayer is not specifically mentioned, prayer and fasting are definitely linked in the OT.

This verse alludes to the mystery of prayer and providence. It is obviously God's will that
the Jewish people survive in order for the Messiah to come. Why then such extraordinary means: (1) fasting
(three days and nights with no food or water, a total fast) and (2) the numbers of people? Will God not
act unless His people humble themselves and pray? God's redemptive will must have priority over human action!
Does this whole context imply that God will surely accomplish His purposes, but possibly not through Esther
and Mordecai (cf. Esth. 4:14)?

These questions are mysteries. Mystery about

- a sovereign God and a covenant people

- prayer and providence

- the new modern theological emphasis on open-theism (cf. Clark Pinnock, The Most Moved Mover

Special Topic:
Predestination (Calvinism) vs Human Free Will (Arminianism)
